cards.myth: Buying before you sell means you need bridging finance.
cards.reality: Lining up both settlements usually does the same job, cheaper.
cards.because: A bridge can cost thousands while you carry two loans. Match the settlement dates or use equity in an offset. Bridge only for a long gap.

posts.linkedin:
Bridging finance is usually the expensive way to solve a timing problem.

Buying before you sell feels like it needs a bridging loan. Most of the time it doesn't. While a bridge runs you're carrying the old loan and the new one, and that can cost thousands.

So we look at cheaper fixes first. If the two settlements are only days or weeks apart, we negotiate the dates so they land together and you move once. If you have equity, an offset or line of credit can often cover the gap.

Bridging earns its place when there's a long gap between the sale and the purchase. Not a few days.

Before you sign up for one, ask whether matching the settlement dates gets you there instead.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.hook: Want a better rate on business funding? Offer security.
cards.so_what: Ask how much partial security, even 30–40% of the limit, would move the price before taking the first quote.

posts.linkedin:
Want a better rate on business funding? Offer security.

On bigger trade and working-capital facilities, the fees across the major banks tend to look much the same. What actually moves the price is security.

It doesn't have to be everything. Partial cover, often around 30 to 40 percent of the limit, gives a bank a lot of comfort. That can be property, or cash such as a term deposit held with the bank.

So before you accept the first quote on a facility of any real size, ask the question most owners skip: how much would the rate change if we offered some security? Then decide whether that trade-off suits you.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.text:
Cash in a savings account is working for the bank, not you.

Most people keep savings and the home loan in separate boxes. One pays a little. The other charges a lot.

An offset puts them in the same box. The money stays yours to spend, and every dollar stops interest on the loan.

We'd rather your cash argued with your mortgage than sat quietly next to it.

posts.linkedin:
Cash in a savings account is working for the bank, not you.

We see it all the time: a healthy savings balance earning a little interest, sitting next to a home loan charging a lot more. And the interest you earn is usually taxable.

Move the same money into an offset linked to your mortgage and it reduces the interest you're charged on the loan instead. It's still your money, still there when you need it. How the tax side works for you is one for your accountant.

If you have savings and a home loan at the same time, ask what moving that cash into an offset would save you each month.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.hook: Buying your first home this year? Sort these three first.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Take the permanent role
cards.body: Changing jobs anyway? A permanent salary can count almost straight away. Contract income is treated like self-employed income and needs a track record, which can push your purchase back a year.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Clear the car loan first
cards.body: Got savings and a car loan? Paying it out before you apply is often worth it, even with a break fee. Those repayments eat into what you can borrow.

cards.label: first home
cards.title: Plan for the first two years
cards.body: Your mortgage feels biggest on day one. Incomes tend to rise and the debt shrinks in real terms. So build your buffer for the first two years, when it bites hardest.

cards.headline: Buying soon? Talk to us before you change anything.
cards.body: A 15-minute chat now can save you months later.

posts.linkedin:
Buying your first home this year? Sort these three things first.

1. Changing jobs anyway? Take the permanent role. A permanent salary can count almost straight away. Contract income is treated like self-employed income and needs a track record, which can push a purchase back by a year.

2. Got savings and a car loan? Clear the car first. Even with a break fee it's often worth it, because those repayments cut what you can borrow.

3. Plan your buffer for the first two years. A mortgage feels biggest on day one. Incomes tend to rise and the debt shrinks in real terms, but the early stretch is when it bites.

If a purchase is close, ask us before you change anything.

General information only, not personal advice.
